questions.q: Name the three biofertilizers discussed in this node and state one key difference in their nitrogen-fixing ability.
questions.a: The three biofertilizers are Rhizobium, Azotobacter, and Mycorrhiza. Rhizobium and Azotobacter fix atmospheric nitrogen (Rhizobium symbiotically in legume nodules, Azotobacter freely in soil), whereas Mycorrhiza does not fix nitrogen — it enhances phosphorus uptake and water absorption. A wrong answer that says "Mycorrhiza fixes nitrogen" reveals confusion between nitrogen fixation and phosphorus solubilization.

questions.q: A farmer applies Rhizobium inoculant to a wheat field. Will it increase soil nitrogen? Explain why or why not.
questions.a: No, Rhizobium will not increase soil nitrogen in wheat because Rhizobium forms nodules only on legume roots (e.g., peas, beans, soybean). Wheat is a non-legume and cannot host Rhizobium. A student who answers "yes" thinks Rhizobium works on all crops — a common misconception that ignores host specificity.

questions.q: You have 1 kg of Azotobacter carrier-based inoculant (10^8 cells/g). The recommended dose is 200 g per acre. How many acres can you treat, and how many viable cells are applied per acre?
questions.a: Step 1: Total inoculant = 1000 g. Step 2: Dose per acre = 200 g. Step 3: Acres treated = 1000 g / 200 g/acre = 5 acres. Step 4: Cells per acre = 200 g × 10^8 cells/g = 2 × 10^10 cells. Answer: 5 acres, 2 × 10^10 cells/acre. A wrong answer that multiplies 1000 g by 10^8 and forgets to divide by dose shows failure to apply unit conversion.

questions.q: Compare the survival challenges of Rhizobium vs. Azotobacter when applied to acidic soil (pH 5.0). Which is more tolerant and why?
questions.a: Rhizobium is highly sensitive to low pH; most strains die below pH 6.0 because acidic conditions denature nitrogenase and damage cell membranes. Azotobacter tolerates pH down to ~5.5 due to its thick cyst walls and production of alginate slime that buffers pH. Thus Azotobacter is more tolerant. A student who says "both die equally" misses the physiological adaptation difference.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "Mycorrhiza can replace chemical phosphorus fertilizer completely in all crops." Defend or refute with two reasons.
questions.a: Refute. Reason 1: Mycorrhiza mobilizes existing soil phosphorus but cannot create phosphorus de novo; in severely P-deficient soils, external P is still needed. Reason 2: Mycorrhizal colonization varies by crop (e.g., brassicas are non-mycorrhizal) and soil conditions (high P fertilizer suppresses colonization). A student who agrees overlooks the dependency on native soil P and host compatibility.

questions.q: Design a small experiment to test whether a local isolate of Azotobacter fixes nitrogen more efficiently than a commercial strain. List the control, measurable variable, and one precaution.
questions.a: Control: Uninoculated sterile soil with same carbon source. Measurable variable: Acetylene reduction assay (ARA) rate (nmol C2H4/h/g soil) or total nitrogen increase by Kjeldahl after 30 days. Precaution: Maintain microaerophilic conditions (2–5% O2) because nitrogenase is O2-sensitive. A poor answer that uses "plant height" as the only measure confuses biofertilizer effect with plant genetics.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: ______ are microorganisms that enhance soil fertility by fixing atmospheric nitrogen, solubilizing phosphorus, or decomposing organic matter; Rhizobium forms symbiotic nodules on legume roots to fix nitrogen, Azotobacter fixes nitrogen freely in the rhizosphere of non-legumes, and Mycorrhiza (fungal hyphae) extends root surface area for improved phosphorus uptake and water absorption.
Fill in the blank: Imagine a farmer in Punjab who grows wheat after harvesting rice — he notices declining yields ______ adding urea.
What is Biofertilizers? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Biofertilizers are microorganisms that enhance soil fertility by fixing atmospheric nitrogen, solubilizing phosphorus, or decomposing organic matter; Rhizobium forms symbiotic nodules on legume roots to fix nitrogen, Azotobacter fixes nitrogen freely in the rhizosphere of non-legumes, and Mycorrhiza (fungal hyphae) extends root surface.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Biofertilizers?
questions.a: Students often write "Rhizobium fixes nitrogen in the soil for all plants" — they treat Rhizobium as a general soil fertilizer like urea.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can (1) distinguish between symbiotic (Rhizobium), free-living (Azotobacter), and fungal (Mycorrhiza) biofertilizers by their mode of action and host specificity, and (2) explain how each contributes to soil nitrogen/phosphorus economy with at least one crop example per type.
